en: To combine or unite into one
hook: AMALGAMATE: A MALL that GATHERs many shops into one.
story: Amalgamate. Two small banks in Chattogram were both struggling. Each had loyal customers but too little capital. Their boards met and agreed to join together as one larger bank, with a new name, one head office, and one set of accounts. They amalgamated. To amalgamate is to combine or unite into one. In chemistry, an amalgam is mercury mixed with another metal, like the silver tooth fillings dentists once used. Synonyms: merge, fuse, consolidate. Opposite: separate.

gre.s: Rather than keep the three struggling departments separate, the dean decided to ____ them into a single school with one budget and one administration.
gre.clue: into a single school with one budget and one administration

example: Over the summer, Farhana amalgamated her scattered lab notes into one tidy spreadsheet that the whole research group could use.

en: To state or assert something to be true, firmly
hook: AVER: 'A-VERity', declaring the truth.
story: Aver. In the courtroom, the lawyer asked the witness whether she was certain. She looked straight at the judge. "I saw him with my own eyes. He was there at ten o'clock. I am completely sure." She averred it: she stated firmly that it was true. Aver is a formal word, common in law and argument. It comes from Latin verus, true, as in verify and verity: to aver is to declare something true. Synonyms: assert, affirm, maintain. Opposite: deny.

gre.s: Even under intense cross-examination, the witness continued to ____ that she had seen the defendant at the scene, never once wavering from her account.
gre.clue: never once wavering from her account

example: In her memoir, the retired cricketer avers that she never once considered quitting, even after the injury that ended her season.

en: Doing good; generous and kind
hook: BENE = good, FIC = do. Doing good.
story: Beneficent. A businessman who grew up poor in a Kishoreganj village returned thirty years later as a millionaire. Quietly, he built three schools, a hospital, and a library. When the villagers wanted to name the buildings after him, he refused. "Name them after your mothers," he said. He was beneficent: actively doing good, generous and charitable. Bene means good, fic means do. Benevolent means wishing good; beneficent means actually doing it.

gre.s: The ____ foundation has funded clean-water projects in over forty countries, asking nothing in return from the communities it serves.
gre.clue: asking nothing in return from the communities it serves

example: A beneficent neighbor in Mirpur quietly paid for the medicines of every elderly resident on our lane.

en: The use of clever trickery to deceive
hook: CHICANERY: a CHICKEN-sly fox's trick.
story: Chicanery. The company's advertisement promised to double your money in three months. Smiling agents visited villages with glossy brochures and fake testimonials. Retired teachers and farmers handed over their life savings. Then, one Monday, the office was empty and the phones were dead. The founders had flown abroad. The whole scheme had been chicanery: clever trickery used to deceive people, especially in business, law, or politics. Picture a sly fox tricking a chicken out of its eggs.

gre.s: The lawyer's courtroom victories owed less to sound argument than to ____: misleading exhibits, coached witnesses, and procedural tricks.
gre.clue: misleading exhibits, coached witnesses, and procedural tricks

example: The election commission annulled the result after finding evidence of chicanery, including ballot boxes that had been stuffed overnight.

en: To share in someone's sadness and show them sympathy
hook: COM-MISERATE: share someone's MISERY.
story: Commiserate. After the exam results came out, Rumana and her friends sat on the hostel roof. Three of them had failed the same difficult course. They shared tea, complained about the impossible questions, and comforted one another until midnight. They were commiserating: expressing sympathy and sorrow for each other. Com means with, and miser means wretched, as in misery, so to commiserate is to share someone's misery. Synonyms: sympathize, console, condole.

gre.s: When the factory closed, former coworkers gathered every evening at the tea stall to ____ with one another over lost wages and uncertain futures.
gre.clue: over lost wages and uncertain futures

example: After the exam results were posted, the friends met at a cafe in Dhanmondi to commiserate about the brutal physics paper.

en: To sing in a low, gentle, tender voice
hook: CROON: like a CROONER singing softly into the moon.
story: Croon. Late at night on the river, an old boatman rows slowly and croons a bhatiali song, soft and low, his voice drifting across the dark water. In a house on the bank, Kamal's mother croons a lullaby until the baby falls asleep. To croon is to sing or hum softly and sentimentally. In the 1940s, smooth, gentle singers like Frank Sinatra were called crooners. Think of a voice that coos rather than shouts. Synonyms: hum, warble, murmur.

gre.s: Rather than belting out the song as most performers did, he chose to ____ it softly, turning the rousing anthem into an intimate lullaby.
gre.clue: Rather than belting out the song

example: As the ferry drifted down the river at dusk, an old boatman crooned a folk song under his breath.

en: A bad-tempered, grumpy person, especially an old one
hook: CURMUDGEON: a grumpy old CUR (dog) growling in the MUD.
story: Curmudgeon. Old Mr Karim in flat 3B complains about everything. The children are too noisy, the lift is too slow, the tea is too sweet, and modern music is a crime. When neighbours wish him a happy Eid, he grumbles that holidays are a waste of time. He is a curmudgeon: a bad-tempered, grumpy person, especially an old one. Picture a snarling cur, a stray dog, muttering at everyone who passes. Synonyms: grouch, crank, grump.

gre.s: Though he cultivated a reputation as a ____, grumbling at visitors and scowling in photographs, the old professor quietly paid the tuition of dozens of poor students.
gre.clue: grumbling at visitors and scowling in photographs

example: Every library seems to have one curmudgeon who glares at anyone whispering, yet ours also kept a jar of sweets for children.

en: A calming of tensions between rival nations
hook: DETENTE: like DE-TENSE, reducing tension.
story: Detente. During the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union aimed thousands of nuclear missiles at each other. In the 1970s, their leaders began signing arms agreements, trading grain, and even flying a joint space mission. That period of relaxed tension was called detente: the easing of hostility between countries. Detente is French for loosening, like releasing a tightly drawn bowstring. Its opposite is escalation. Synonyms: rapprochement, thaw.

gre.s: After decades of border skirmishes, the two neighbors entered a period of ____, reopening trade routes and exchanging ambassadors for the first time in a generation.
gre.clue: reopening trade routes and exchanging ambassadors

example: The brief detente between the superpowers in the 1970s produced arms treaties and even a joint space mission.

en: A stretch of talk or writing that strays off the main topic
hook: DIGRESSION: DIGS off the main path.
story: Digression. Professor Latif began a lecture on the Mughal economy, then mentioned his trip to Agra, then the sweets he ate there, then his grandmother's cooking. Twenty minutes later he laughed and said, "Where was I? Ah yes, taxes." His students loved these digressions: temporary departures from the main subject. The verb is digress. Di means apart, and gress means step, as in progress: stepping aside from the path. Synonyms: tangent, aside, detour.

gre.s: Though the biography is generally tightly focused, its author indulges in an occasional ____, wandering away from her subject's life to discuss the history of the region.
gre.clue: wandering away from her subject's life

example: Halfway through the budget meeting, a long digression about the office cricket team ate up twenty minutes.

en: To free from something that is tangled or complicated
hook: DIS-ENTANGLE: undo the TANGLE.
story: Disentangle. Priya opened her drawer and found her earphones, phone charger, and a necklace knotted together in one hopeless ball. She sat on her bed for twenty minutes, patiently untwisting each strand until all three were free. She had disentangled them: freed them from a tangle. The word is often used for complicated situations too: a lawyer disentangles a messy family property dispute, separating each claim. Dis means undo: to disentangle is to undo a tangle. Synonyms: untangle, extricate, unravel.

gre.s: It took the auditors nearly a year to ____ the company's true finances from a web of shell companies and deliberately misleading accounts.
gre.clue: a web of shell companies and deliberately misleading accounts

example: Historians still struggle to disentangle the legends about the medieval king from the facts recorded in surviving documents.

en: To push or encourage someone forcefully to act
hook: EX-HORT: like a coach shouting 'HURT now, win later!'
story: Exhort. On the night before the final, the captain of the university football team gathered his exhausted players. 'We have trained for a year,' he said, his voice rising. 'Tomorrow, run until you cannot run anymore. Do it for everyone who believed in us.' He exhorted them: he strongly urged them to act. Exhort is stronger than suggest; it is urging with passion. Preachers exhort their congregations, and coaches exhort their teams. Synonyms: urge, implore, spur.

gre.s: Health workers went from door to door to ____ families to boil their drinking water, warning that the cholera outbreak could otherwise spread rapidly.
gre.clue: warning that the cholera outbreak could otherwise spread rapidly

example: Before the final, the captain exhorted her teammates to forget the scoreboard and simply play their own game.

en: Starting and stopping unevenly instead of continuing steadily
hook: FITFUL: in FITS and starts.
story: Fitful. On the night before her GRE, Rumana's sleep was fitful. She drifted off, woke at one, dozed again, woke at three to check the alarm, then lay staring at the ceiling until dawn. Her sleep came in irregular bursts, never steady. Fitful means occurring in irregular bursts, stopping and starting. Think of the phrase fits and starts. A fitful wind gusts and then dies; fitful progress lurches forward, then stalls. Synonyms: intermittent, sporadic, erratic.

gre.s: Progress on the bridge has been ____ at best, with long stretches of inactivity interrupted by brief bursts of construction whenever funds arrived.
gre.clue: long stretches of inactivity interrupted by brief bursts

example: Worried about his job interview, Tanvir drifted in and out of fitful sleep until the call to prayer woke him.

en: To break a rule or custom boldly and in plain view
hook: FLOUT the rule, FLAUNT the attitude: breaking it proudly in public.
story: Flout. The sign at the exam hall door was huge and red: No Phones. One candidate sat in the waiting room, scrolling openly, laughing at videos while the guard watched him. He was not hiding anything. He simply did not care. To flout a rule is to break it boldly and in public, as if it does not exist. Do not confuse it with flaunt, which means to show off. You flout the rules; you flaunt your new watch.

gre.s: Rather than quietly ignoring the dress code, the students chose to ____ it openly, arriving in costumes that mocked the regulations.
gre.clue: Rather than quietly ignoring

example: Bus drivers who flout the lane rules on Airport Road now face heavy fines under the new traffic law.

en: Lazy; avoiding activity or work
hook: INDOLENT: IN DOLE, living lazily on handouts without work.
story: Indolent. Tanvir's roommate slept until noon, ordered food instead of cooking, and left dishes piling up in the sink for a week. The fan blew dust across his unopened textbooks. When Tanvir asked him to help clean, he groaned, rolled over, and said, "Tomorrow." Tomorrow never came. He was indolent: habitually lazy, avoiding any effort. Indolent is a fancier synonym of slothful and idle, and a favourite GRE word.

gre.s: The governor was criticized as ____, preferring long holidays to the tedious work of governing while problems mounted at home.
gre.clue: preferring long holidays to the tedious work of governing

example: The heat of the long afternoon made even the usually busy market traders indolent, dozing beside their stalls.

en: Disliking and distrusting people in general
hook: MIS = hate, ANTHROP = human. Hating humans.
story: Misanthropic. Old Mr. Haque lived alone at the end of the lane. When children played cricket, he slammed his windows. He refused every wedding invitation and muttered that people were selfish, noisy, and stupid. Yet every morning he fed the stray cats, talking to them softly. He disliked humans, not animals. That is misanthropic: distrusting and disliking humanity in general. Mis means hate, anthrop means human. The opposite is a philanthropist, who loves people and gives generously.

gre.s: The writer's later essays reveal a deeply ____ outlook; she came to regard human nature as fundamentally selfish and cruel.
gre.clue: regard human nature as fundamentally selfish and cruel

example: Years of watching colleagues betray one another left the detective in the novel bitter and misanthropic.

en: Sharply sarcastic or critical
hook: MORDANT: it BITES (Latin mordere, to bite).
story: Mordant. The comedian on the late-night show was famous for his mordant humour. He described a minister's new policy as "a solution looking for a problem" and a celebrity's memoir as "three hundred pages of mirrors." The audience laughed and winced at the same time. Mordant means sharply sarcastic and biting. In Latin, mordere means to bite. A mordant critic's words sting long after you have stopped laughing. Synonyms: caustic, acerbic.

gre.s: The columnist's ____ wit spared no one, and politicians dreaded seeing their names in her biting weekly column.
gre.clue: politicians dreaded seeing their names in her biting weekly column

example: The comedian's mordant jokes about the city's endless traffic jams drew both laughter and complaints from officials.

en: Pleasantly sharp or spicy in taste; lively and interesting
hook: PIQUANT (PEE-kunt): it PIQUES your tastebuds.
story: Piquant. Lamia's grandmother makes a famous fish curry with green chilies, mustard, and a squeeze of lime. The first bite is sharp and spicy, then tangy and fresh, and everyone asks for more. Her curry is piquant: having a pleasantly sharp, spicy taste. Piquant can also describe something stimulating and interesting, like a piquant bit of gossip. It comes from the French piquer, to prick or sting. Synonyms: tangy, zesty, spicy; or intriguing, provocative.

gre.s: Though the biography covers familiar territory, its ____ anecdotes about the poet's feuds and love affairs keep readers engaged from beginning to end.
gre.clue: keep readers engaged from beginning to end

example: Nusrat's grandmother adds tamarind and green chili to the chutney, giving it a piquant edge that guests always praise.

en: To split people into two strongly opposed sides
bn: মেরুকরণ করা; দুই বিপরীত দলে বিভক্ত করা
hook: POLARIZE: pushes people to opposite POLES, north and south.
story: Polarize. During the World Cup, Priya's class split in two. Half the students wore Argentina shirts; half wore Brazil shirts. Lunch tables divided. Friendships cooled. Even the teachers took sides. Nobody, absolutely nobody, stood in the middle. The tournament had polarized the class: split it into two sharply opposing groups, like the north and south poles of a magnet. Political issues often polarize whole countries, leaving no room for moderate voices.

gre.s: Rather than unite the party, the leader's divisive speech threatened to ____ its members into two hostile camps.
gre.clue: into two hostile camps

example: The proposal to close the old stadium polarized the town, setting longtime fans against the developers.

en: Deep wisdom, understanding, or intensity of feeling
hook: PROFUNDITY = PROFOUND-ity.
story: Profundity. Rabindranath Tagore wrote songs about the most ordinary things: rain on a tin roof, a boat on a river, a child waiting for her father. Yet every line carries surprising profundity about love, loss, and the meaning of life. Readers return to them at eighty and find depths they missed at eighteen. Profundity means great depth of insight, knowledge, or feeling. It comes from profound. Its opposite is superficiality.

gre.s: The essay's apparent simplicity conceals real ____; its short sentences reward readers who return to them again and again.
gre.clue: reward readers who return to them again and again

example: Listeners were struck by the profundity of the young poet's reflections on grief, which seemed far beyond her years.

en: Suggesting that things are likely to go well
hook: PROPITIOUS: PROPER time to act — the signs are favorable.
story: Propitious. Farmers in Rangpur waited anxiously for the planting season. Then the rains arrived on time, the soil was soft, fertiliser prices fell, and new seeds came from the research institute. Everything pointed to a good harvest. The conditions were propitious: favourable, indicating a good chance of success. Propitious comes from the Latin for gracious, as if the gods were smiling on you. Its close cousin is auspicious. Synonyms: favourable, opportune, promising.

gre.s: Investors were wary of launching the venture during a recession, but the sudden drop in interest rates made the moment unexpectedly ____.
gre.clue: the sudden drop in interest rates

example: Clear skies and calm winds offered a propitious morning for the fishing boats setting out from Cox's Bazar.

en: To break a promise or fail to keep a deal
hook: RENEGE: RE-NEG(ATE) your promise.
story: Renege. Before the election, a candidate promised Imran's village a new bridge. He shook hands with the elders and even laid a foundation stone. After winning, he announced that the money would go to a highway instead. He had reneged on his promise: gone back on it. Renege is almost always followed by on. Hear the word negative inside it: reneging is saying no to what you once said yes to. Synonyms: backtrack, default, go back.

gre.s: Having promised in writing to fund the new library, the company later tried to ____ on the deal, claiming the agreement had never been binding.
gre.clue: claiming the agreement had never been binding

example: The landlord reneged on his promise to repair the leaking roof before the monsoon, leaving the tenants furious.

en: An unintended consequence, often bad, of an event or action
hook: RE-PERCUSSION: like a drum's echo, the effect bounces back.
story: Repercussion. When a neighbouring country suddenly banned onion exports, onion prices in Dhaka doubled within a week. Restaurants raised their prices, families cut back, and street food sellers lost customers. These were the repercussions of one decision made far away: unintended, often bad consequences. Think of percussion, like a drum: a repercussion is the echo that bounces back after the first strike. Repercussions often spread far beyond the original event. Synonyms: consequence, aftermath, fallout.

gre.s: One unforeseen ____ of the ban on plastic bags was a sudden shortage of jute sacks, as demand far outstripped what local mills could supply.
gre.clue: unforeseen

example: Few lawmakers foresaw the repercussions of the tax cut, which eventually forced deep reductions in school funding.

en: A person with no morals who behaves badly
hook: REPROBATE: REPROVED and BEATEN by society.
story: Reprobate. Everyone in the neighborhood knew Babu's uncle. He gambled away his wife's jewelry, borrowed money from every relative without repaying a taka, lied to the police, and laughed about it all at the tea stall. The elders called him a reprobate: an unprincipled person, beyond moral correction. The word comes from the Latin for disapproved or rejected; in old religious language, a reprobate was someone damned. Synonyms: scoundrel, rogue, miscreant, degenerate.

gre.s: Though the novel's hero is a charming ____ who lies, gambles, and abandons his debts, readers cannot help hoping that he will escape justice.
gre.clue: who lies, gambles, and abandons his debts

example: The village elders dismissed the returning nephew as a reprobate, remembering the debts and lies he had left behind.

en: Messy and careless in appearance or work
hook: SLOVENLY: SLOPPY and LOVE-less care.
story: Slovenly. Sabbir's hostel room was famous. Dirty socks hung from the ceiling fan, rice plates sat under the bed for days, and his shirts were always wrinkled and half tucked in. His lab reports looked the same, with tea stains, crossed out numbers and missing units. His teacher finally wrote at the top: "Brilliant ideas, slovenly work." Slovenly means messy and careless, in appearance or in work. Think of a sloppy sloth that never cleans. Synonyms: untidy, sloppy, unkempt.

gre.s: The editor rejected the manuscript not for its ideas but for its ____ presentation: pages were out of order, quotations were unattributed, and typos littered every paragraph.
gre.clue: typos littered every paragraph

example: The inspector criticized the kitchen's slovenly habits, noting greasy counters and vegetables left rotting in open crates.

en: Someone who cannot save and throws money away freely
hook: SPEND-THRIFT: spends away all the thrift (savings).
story: Spendthrift. On the first day of every month, Tanvir's salary arrived. By the seventh, it was gone: new sneakers, restaurant dinners, a gaming headset he used twice. By the twentieth, he was borrowing money from his younger sister, who had saved half of her much smaller salary. "You are a spendthrift," she told him, counting out notes. A spendthrift spends money recklessly, wasting everything they have. The opposite is a miser, who refuses to spend at all.

gre.s: The heir was a notorious ____, squandering in three years a fortune that his frugal grandfather had spent decades accumulating.
gre.clue: squandering in three years a fortune

example: My cousin was such a spendthrift that his monthly salary from the bank vanished on gadgets within a week.

en: To mark someone as disgraceful or shameful
hook: STIGMA = a mark of shame.
story: Stigmatize. For years in many communities, people who visited a psychiatrist were gossiped about and labelled crazy. Families hid relatives' illnesses out of shame, and many people suffered silently rather than seek help. Mental illness was stigmatized: marked as shameful and disgraceful. A stigma is a mark of shame. Today, campaigns, doctors, and brave public figures work to remove that stigma so that people feel free to ask for help.

gre.s: Advocates argue that requiring patients to register publicly would only ____ them further, discouraging others from seeking treatment.
gre.clue: discouraging others from seeking treatment

example: Older laws stigmatized children born outside marriage, denying them inheritance and labeling them in public records.

en: Far more of something than is needed or wanted
hook: SURFEIT: SURplus, FEasting too much.
story: Surfeit. At his cousin's wedding, Babu ate three plates of biryani, two bowls of roast chicken, a mountain of rezala, and four bowls of sweet yogurt. That night he could not sleep and swore he would never eat again. He had suffered from a surfeit: an excessive amount of something. It comes from old French words meaning overdone. Its opposite is dearth, a shortage. Surfeit can also be a verb: surfeited with food. Synonyms: excess, glut, overabundance.

gre.s: Far from suffering from a shortage of information, modern voters face a ____ of it, so much that they struggle to separate reliable facts from noise.
gre.clue: so much that they struggle to separate reliable facts from noise

example: A surfeit of mangoes in June drives prices so low in Rajshahi that some growers leave fruit unpicked.

en: To get past or defeat a problem or barrier
hook: SUR-MOUNT: climb OVER the MOUNTain.
story: Surmount. Babu was born on a char, a sandy island in the Jamuna that floods every year. His school had no electricity, so he studied by a kerosene lamp, and more than once the river washed away his books. Yet he surmounted every obstacle and won a place at a top engineering university. To surmount is to overcome a difficulty or obstacle. Sur means over and mount means climb, as in mountain: to surmount is to climb over. Synonyms: overcome, conquer, transcend.

gre.s: Experts doubted that the climbers could ____ the final ice wall, which had turned back every previous expedition; yet the team reached the summit before noon.
gre.clue: which had turned back every previous expedition

example: Born with poor eyesight, the scholar surmounted every barrier to become the first in her family to earn a doctorate.

en: Easily handled, guided, or controlled
hook: TRACTABLE: easily pulled, like a TRACTOR pulling a cart.
story: Tractable. Joya's new puppy was a dream. Within one week it learned to sit, stay, and wait patiently for food. It walked politely on its leash and came running when called. The neighbour's dog, by contrast, ignored every command and once ate a shoe. The puppy was tractable: easy to control and manage. A tractable problem can be solved. An intractable conflict, like a stubborn dog, refuses every attempt at control.

gre.s: Once considered ____, the problem has resisted every attempt at a solution for over forty years, baffling the best mathematicians.
gre.clue: has resisted every attempt at a solution for over forty years

example: Breaking the huge coding project into small tasks made it far more tractable for the new team of interns.

en: To honor someone or something with great respect
hook: VENERATE: like VENUS, treated as a goddess.
story: Venerate. For forty years, Master Moshai taught mathematics in a village school in Netrokona. He never took a single taka for extra lessons, walked miles to visit sick students, and taught three generations of the same families. When he died, the whole district came to his funeral, and people still touch his photograph in the school hall. The village venerates him: regards him with deep respect and reverence, almost like worship.

gre.s: Many cultures ____ their elders, consulting them on important decisions and honoring them in elaborate ceremonies.
gre.clue: honoring them in elaborate ceremonies

example: Musicians across Bengal still venerate Lalon Shah, singing his songs at the yearly gathering in Kushtia.
